processing: Seven stages: sun-withering, cooling, shaking, resting, fixing, rolling and drying, with five or six rounds of shaking and resting across about 18 hours. Oxidation runs higher than in greener oolongs.
harvest_season: Picking dates are not well documented; spring is the main season across the Phoenix area.
appearance_dry: Fine, tight strands with an oily green tone.
appearance_wet: Tender green leaf with a thin red line along the edge; the leaves are thicker than most Shuixian types.
taste_profile: Ripe honey and fruit on the nose, then a round, creamy, fairly sweet body with a long, clean finish.

brewing.notes: General oolong approach, as no standard method is recorded for this tea. Small teapot or gaiwan with hot water; it is said to hold its flavour across many infusions.

vintage_note: Sold as a recent-harvest oolong, in very small quantities from a handful of producers. A Chinese description says new tea holds its colour, aroma and flavour for a year in storage, so a lot of last year's picking is not necessarily stale. No regular aged market is documented.
description:
Shi Gu Ping is the odd one out on Phoenix Mountain. It comes from a She ethnic village above Fenghuang town, and the tea is made from a local oolong variety rather than the Shuixian family behind almost all dancong.

The thick leaf takes the traditional shaking well: five or six rounds of shaking and resting across about 18 hours, then fixing, rolling and drying. Tea writer Leo Kwan describes it as more oxidised than greener oolongs, and credits the shaking for its body.

Expect honey and ripe fruit with a round, creamy mouthfeel and a long, clean end. Descriptions of colour do vary: a Chinese account gives a yellow-green liquor and a green-toned leaf, so lots may differ by maker. Brew it hot in a small pot.

Very few people still make it, so it is hard to find.
history:
Shiguping is a She village at the foot of the third-highest peak in the Phoenix range, and She people in Fujian and Zhejiang regard it as an ancestral home. A local saying holds that no She mountain goes without tea gardens. The legend of She villagers giving tea to the fleeing Song emperor Zhao Bing belongs to the wider Phoenix area and is a folk tale.

When oolong making began here is not firmly documented. Kwan suggests the local variety is very old and possibly a predecessor of the Minnan and Taiwanese groups, which is his own opinion rather than an established finding. It is listed among Guangdong's well-known teas, but only a handful of producers remain.
